newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shoots seven Palestinians in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shoots seven Palestinians in Hebron.

text.p: An Israeli soldier firing indiscriminately wounded seven Arabs in a Hebron market on Wednesday in an attempt to sabotage the imminent handover of the West Bank town to Palestinian rule.
The off-duty soldier, who lives in a settlement near Jerusalem, emptied the clip of his M-16 automatic rifle into the crowded open-air market before other soldiers overpowered him, witnesses said.
"Even after soldiers had wrestled him to the ground he tried to put a second magazine into his gun," said Reuters cameraman Mazen Dana.

The conscript, wearing the skullcap and tassled undershirt of a religious Jew beneath his uniform, sprayed bullets for several seconds into the vegetable market on Martyrs Street wounding men, women and a youth, witnesses and doctors said. Two of the injured were in critical condition.

Palestinians hurled themselves to the ground shouting "massacre" when the bullets started flying. Soldiers and police, thinking they were under attack, ran to the market from the Avraham Avinu settlement firing, witnesses said. One Palestinian man was apparently hit by them.
The army poured troops into the city and put armoured personnel carriers on surrounding hills to prevent reprisals.

Youths burned tyres and clashed with soldiers briefly after the shooting but the streets quickly emptied. Soldiers beat back a crowd that gathered at the market after the shooting, the worst in the city since settler Baruch Goldstein massacred 29 Moslems at prayer three years ago.
Israeli security sources identified the gunman as Noam Friedman from the Maale Adumim settlement near Jerusalem. One source said he was 19 years old.

The shooting underscored the fragility of the U.S.-sponsored Middle East peace process and the feeling of betrayal of right-wing Jews opposed to returning captured land to Arabs. It was another religious Jew, Yigal Amir, who tried to stop land-for-peace deals by assassinating prime minister Yitzhak Rabin 14 months ago.
The United States deplored the shooting and vowed to continue mediating a settlement on the long-delayed Israeli redeployment from 80 percent of Hebron.

"We in the United States condemn this act in the strongest possible terms," U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross told reporters in Gaza after meeting Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. Asked if talks would continue, Ross said: "Yes".
Ross met earlier with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who also condemned the attack.

Ross is trying to arrange an Arafat-Netanyahu summit to close the Hebron deal. PLO officials said Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas and Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai would meet later in the day in an effort to keep talks on track.
"I want to say again in a sharp way that no crime and no violent act will stand in the way of our completing the work," Netanyahu told reporters in Jerusalem.

The gunman told investigators he wanted to sabotage the handover, Israel's central area commander Major-General Uzi Dayan said. The centre of the city, where some 400 Jewish settlers live in heavily guarded enclaves among 100,000 Arabs, was closed.
Hebron has been a powderkeg since the Goldstein massacre in the al-Ibrahimi mosque at the Cave of the Patriarchs, a site holy to Jews and Moslems.

"It happened right in front of me," said vegetable seller Walid Kafisheh, 46, on Wednesday. "I tried to stop him but the soldiers got to him first. Then soldiers and police came from everywhere shooting," he told Reuters.
Israeli lieutenant Avi Buskila grabbed the soldier.

"He entered the area at the square and began shooting into the vegetable market. I stood at my post and heard the shots. Within 10 seconds I pinned him to the ground and took his gun," he told Reuters.

Jewish settlers in the town had said they were praying for a miracle to prevent Israeli troops from pulling back and warned of impending bloodshed. They scuffled with Palestinians on Tuesday and tried to take over Arab houses in the casbah.
Jewish settlers, who number 130,000 in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, helped Netanyahu sweep to power in elections last May on a promise to be tough with the Palestinians.

But Netanyahu has come under pressure from Washington, Israel's closest ally, to honour peace deals and withdraw from Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns due for self-rule under the first stage of the 1993 Oslo peace accord.
